strengths: The paper addresses an important gap by introducing a large-scale multilingual chart QA benchmark covering 22,606 charts, 26,151 QA pairs, ten languages from diverse families, and sixteen chart types, including non-Latin and right-to-left scripts.

The decoupled representation of chart data as JSON plus executable Plotly templates is a sensible and scalable design. Jointly translating the chart specification and associated QA pairs better preserves terminology and semantic alignment than translating question text alone.

The pipeline includes multiple quality-control stages: code executability checks, visual-fidelity comparison, QA-validity checks, back-translation, LLM-based consistency scoring, and human evaluation. The appendix provides unusually detailed prompts and dataset statistics.

The empirical evaluation is broad, comparing closed-source, open-source, general-purpose, and multilingual LVLM families across model sizes, zero-shot and few-shot settings, and three cross-lingual configurations. The findings on native-input superiority and the cost of language mismatch between questions and visuals are useful for future multilingual multimodal work.
The resource is clearly relevant to computational linguistics and NLP and is likely to support research on more globally inclusive vision-language models.
weaknesses: Human validation is concentrated on the English–Chinese subset. For the other nine languages, quality claims rely mainly on Gemini-based proxy judgments and automatic back-translation checks. Strong performance on Chinese does not establish that the proxy is equally reliable for Arabic, Hindi, Bengali, Urdu, or other typologically different languages.

All charts originate from English data and are machine-translated, so the benchmark may contain translationese and English-centered content rather than culturally grounded, natively authored charts. This limits claims about real-world multilingual chart understanding.

The images are Plotly reconstructions rather than the original source charts. Although semantic checks are performed, differences in visual style, layout complexity, and realism may affect ecological validity.

Cross-language comparisons are potentially confounded because the retained numbers of charts and QA pairs differ substantially across languages. The paper should report results on the common parallel subset available in all languages to ensure that performance gaps reflect language ability rather than different item compositions.

Evaluation rigor could be strengthened. Non-numeric answers use exact matching without clearly described multilingual normalization for morphology, synonyms, transliteration, articles, or language-code switching, and only one model run is reported with no confidence intervals or significance tests.

Because the source datasets are public, contamination of English results is possible. In addition, Gemini is heavily used for data construction and quality control and is itself evaluated, raising a possible model-family advantage; neither issue is analyzed.

The filtering pipeline removes trend, explanatory, subjective, and many complex-comparison questions, narrowing the benchmark toward short factual or numeric answers. The title's broader claim of chart understanding should be qualified, and results should be broken down by reasoning skill or question complexity.

Reproducibility depends on proprietary API versions and prompts. The paper should explicitly guarantee release of the rendered images, JSON specifications, generation code, filtered items, human annotations, raw model outputs, and answer-normalization code.

strengths: The paper addresses a clear and important English-centric bias in chart-understanding benchmarks. PolyChartQA is large in scale, with 22,606 charts and 26,151 QA pairs across 10 languages, including several underrepresented non-Latin and RTL scripts such as Arabic, Urdu, Bengali, and Hindi.

The decoupled representation of chart data as language-neutral JSON plus executable Plotly rendering code is a sensible design for producing aligned multilingual charts. Jointly translating chart metadata and QA pairs also helps preserve terminology between the visualization and questions.
The resource covers 16 chart types, including both common and rarer formats, and provides detailed per-language and per-chart-type statistics in the appendix.

The empirical evaluation is broad: it compares closed-source models, general-purpose open-source LVLMs, and multilingual-specialized models, with zero-shot, few-shot, and cross-lingual settings. The reported performance gaps are likely to be useful for future work.

The pipeline includes more quality control than a naive translation approach, including executable-code checks, visual-fidelity filtering, back-translation, LLM consistency scoring, and an English-Chinese human evaluation. The released prompt templates and annotation interface also improve transparency.
The topic is highly relevant to multilingual multimodal NLP, and the benchmark could become a valuable resource if the remaining validation and evaluation concerns are addressed.
weaknesses: Decisive concern: multilingual data quality is not adequately validated at the scale claimed. Human evaluation is performed only on a 250-example English-Chinese subset, while Gemini is used as a proxy for all other languages. There is no native-speaker audit for Arabic, Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, or the other languages, no reported human-human agreement or chance-corrected agreement, and the very high proportion of perfect scores makes exact agreement look artificially strong. METEOR-based back-translation filtering is also a weak and indirect measure of translation quality.

The charts are LLM-reconstructed Plotly renderings rather than the original ChartQA/ChartX images. Although the authors filter rendering errors, the resulting corpus is synthetic and canonicalized, with possible semantic and visual discrepancies from the source charts. Using models from the same LLM ecosystem for both extraction and validation risks correlated failures. This makes the description of the benchmark as containing real-world charts somewhat misleading.

The Stage 1 rewriting prompt explicitly deletes questions involving trends, explanations, subjective judgments, and complex comparisons whenever they require non-concise answers. This biases the benchmark toward short factual lookup and extraction tasks and conflicts with the paper's framing of holistic chart reasoning. The paper does not provide a question-difficulty or reasoning-type taxonomy, nor retention/deletion rates by question type.

Because every chart and QA pair originates from English and is then translated, the benchmark evaluates cross-lingual transfer on English-centric data, not reasoning over authentic, native-language charts or culturally localized visualizations. The broader 'globally inclusive' claim is therefore overstated.

The evaluation relies on exact matching for non-numeric answers across morphologically rich and non-Latin languages. Answer normalization, synonym handling, punctuation, script normalization, and RTL-specific equivalence are not sufficiently described. The single uniform prompt and single inference run also provide no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance tests for the claimed language gaps.

The cross-lingual conclusions are based only on four Qwen-family models in the dedicated ablation, which is too narrow to support general claims about how current LVLMs allocate attention between question and visual language.

Reproducibility would require an explicit, persistent release of the generated charts, JSON, code, translated QA pairs, filtering logs, model versions, API dates, decoding parameters, and seeds. These details are not clearly provided in the manuscript, although the appendix prompts are helpful.

The paper does not analyze potential training-data contamination from the publicly available ChartQA and ChartX source corpora, which could inflate English performance. There are also several typographical and naming errors, such as 'PloyChartQA' and inconsistent wording, that reduce polish.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap by introducing POLYCHARTQA, a large-scale multilingual chart-QA benchmark covering 22,606 chart images and 26,151 QA pairs across 10 languages, including underrepresented non-Latin and RTL scripts.

The decoupled JSON-plus-rendering-code pipeline is a sensible and extensible design: translating chart specifications and QA pairs jointly helps preserve terminology, numerical values, and semantic alignment between localized text and rendered charts.

The data construction includes multiple quality-control stages, including executable-code checks, visual-fidelity validation, QA-validity checks, back-translation, METEOR filtering, LLM assessment, and human evaluation on an English-Chinese subset.

The empirical study is broad, comparing closed-source, open-source, and multilingual-specialized LVLMs, and it includes zero-shot, few-shot, and cross-lingual transfer settings. The reported English-to-low-resource performance gap is both clear and practically important.

The paper provides substantial supporting material, including per-language and per-chart-type statistics, human-evaluation guidelines, the annotation interface, dataset analyses, and detailed prompt templates.

The work is highly relevant to multimodal NLP and computational linguistics, and the benchmark can support future work on multilingual visual reasoning, OCR, translation robustness, and globally inclusive LVLMs.
weaknesses: All non-English data are produced by machine translation from English seed questions and chart specifications, rather than being naturally authored or culturally localized. The benchmark may therefore contain translationese and retain English-centric chart conventions, which limits claims about genuine multilingual chart understanding.

Quality assurance depends heavily on the same family of large models used in the construction pipeline. Native human verification is reported only for an English-Chinese subset of 250 examples; strong performance of the Gemini proxy on Chinese does not by itself establish equivalent reliability for Arabic, Urdu, Bengali, Hindi, or other scripts.

The final chart images are Plotly reconstructions from extracted JSON rather than the original images. This improves controllability but may reduce ecological validity by simplifying visual styles, layouts, fonts, and real-world chart complexity. The claim that the benchmark contains real-world charts should therefore be qualified.

The evaluation reports only a single run per model, with no confidence intervals, significance testing, or longitudinal version controls for proprietary APIs. Some aggregate differences between models are small and may not be robust.

Answer matching is under-specified for multilingual surface forms: non-numeric answers require exact match, while morphology, transliteration, punctuation, synonymy, and script-specific normalization could materially affect results across the ten languages.

The analysis is mainly aggregate by language. More fine-grained breakdowns by reasoning skill, question category, chart type, OCR failure, translation error, and script complexity would better explain the observed performance gaps. Few-shot and cross-lingual analyses are also limited to Qwen-family models.

Although the appendix improves reproducibility, the manuscript would be strengthened by an explicit data/code release plan, retained and rejected sample counts by language and chart type, exact model-version information, and licenses for all derived artifacts.

There are several minor presentation issues, including inconsistent naming such as PloyChartQA in a figure and appendix, typographical errors, and table values labeled as percentages but presented as decimals.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap by introducing a large-scale 10-language chart QA benchmark covering diverse scripts, 16 chart types, and both test and training splits.

The decoupled JSON/Plotly representation and reusable code make multilingual chart generation scalable; the paper provides detailed pipeline descriptions, prompts, licenses, filtering ratios, and per-language/chart-type statistics.

Quality assurance is substantial, including render-execution checks, visual-fidelity and QA-validity filters, back-translation consistency, manual visual inspection, and bilingual human evaluation with inter-annotator agreement.
The empirical study is broad, evaluating 22 proprietary, open-source, chart-specific, and multilingual LVLMs under zero-shot, cross-lingual modality-alignment, fine-tuning, and data-scaling settings.
Consistent fine-tuning gains, especially for weaker models and lower-resource languages, demonstrate the practical value of the companion training set and support the paper's central findings.
weaknesses: Cross-language comparisons may be confounded by unequal retained sample sizes, such as 3,080 English versus 2,195 Japanese test QA pairs; no balanced common-item intersection or paired per-chart cross-lingual analysis is reported.

Exact string matching for non-numeric answers is problematic in morphologically rich languages because synonyms, transliterations, and alternate phrasing can be penalized; a numeric/non-numeric breakdown and semantic-evaluation robustness check would strengthen the results.

Gemini-2.5-Pro is used for extraction, translation, and several validation stages, creating potential circularity. Independent human semantic validation is sampled, and the stated 20% sampling rate conflicts with the reported 250 items per language.

Because test seeds are derived from public ChartQA and ChartX data, possible benchmark contamination is not fully addressed; translated and regenerated items only partially mitigate this risk, and no decontamination or train-test deduplication analysis is provided.
The charts remain translations of English source material rather than native, culturally situated charts, so translationese and inherited source biases may limit ecological validity.

Reproducibility would benefit from persistent links to released data, JSON, code, and model outputs, as well as variance or significance reporting across the eight runs; the captions for Figures 11 and 12 also appear swapped.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely gap: PolyChartQA is a large-scale ten-language chart-QA resource covering diverse scripts and both high- and low-resource languages, with 22,606 test charts, 26,151 test QA pairs, 16 chart types, and a substantial accompanying training set.

The decoupled JSON/code/translation pipeline is practical and scalable. Reusing rendering code while translating only chart content is a sensible design, and the appendix provides detailed prompts, filtering statistics, source-license information, and dataset statistics.

Quality control is comparatively thorough: code execution, automated visual and QA validation, back-translation consistency checks, rendering inspection, and human review are combined. The 250-instance-per-language human evaluation reports near-ceiling quality scores and strong weighted Cohen's kappa values.

The empirical study is broad, covering proprietary, open-source, chart-specific, and multilingual LVLMs. It includes zero-shot evaluation, cross-lingual modality replacement, fine-tuning, data-scale ablations, English-ratio analysis, two-stage training, and error analysis.

The main findings are useful for the community: existing models have substantial non-English weaknesses, broad multilingual pretraining alone is insufficient for text-rich chart grounding, cross-lingual alignment varies considerably by architecture, and targeted instruction tuning can produce large gains.
weaknesses: Ecological validity is limited because the benchmark consists of English-source charts reconstructed with Plotly and then machine-translated, rather than naturally authored multilingual charts. Translation changes text but does not fully localize data, cultural references, naming conventions, or chart-design conventions, so the task is best interpreted as controlled translated chart QA.

The evaluation metric may distort the central cross-lingual findings. Non-numeric answers require exact string matching, with no reported prediction-side normalization, semantic judge, or human validation of model outputs; valid paraphrases, morphological variants, punctuation differences, and transliterations may be rejected, especially in morphologically rich languages. The 5% relative numerical tolerance is also potentially unstable for values near zero.

Although the languages begin as parallel translations, language-specific filtering leaves substantially different test subsets, for example 3,080 English QA pairs versus 2,195 Japanese pairs. Cross-language score differences are therefore not measured on a strictly common parallel item set; results on the all-language intersection are needed to separate language ability from item-selection effects.

There is a possible contamination risk because test questions and underlying tables come from public ChartQA and ChartX splits that may occur in model pretraining. Re-rendering reduces visual memorization but does not remove textual or tabular leakage. No contamination audit, nearest-neighbor deduplication, or detailed train/test overlap analysis across ChartQA, ChartLlama, and ChartX is provided.

The pipeline depends heavily on closed commercial models, especially Gemini-2.5-Pro for extraction, translation, and quality assessment, while Gemini is also the highest-scoring evaluated system. This creates possible selection or familiarity bias. API versions, query dates, raw model outputs, and complete released artifacts are needed for full reproducibility.

The provenance and quality control of the 751K-pair training split are less clear than for the test split. Its relationship to the much larger source datasets and the associated subsampling/filtering rates are underspecified, and the appendix states that detailed training-set filtering statistics were not recorded.

Statistical reporting could be stronger. The text says 22 models whereas Table 3 lists 26 model configurations; results over eight runs do not report variance or significance tests; and the manual error analysis lacks a detailed taxonomy, sampling frame, and inter-annotator agreement.

Fine-tuning improvements are demonstrated only on the benchmark generated by the same pipeline and templates. Evaluation on independent, authentic multilingual chart datasets would be needed to support stronger claims about real-world generalization and the practical impact of PolyChartQA-Train.
